title: ICPC Notebook Java
subtitle: A progressive team reference for Java 17
conventions: Ranges are half-open [left, right) unless documented otherwise.
Check overflow, input bounds, and recursion depth before using a snippet.
Choose the simplest algorithm that fits the problem constraints.

quickReference.signal: All subsets of a small set
Assign left items to right items
Binary pairwise energy with submodular costs
Large polynomial product with safe rounding
Repeated nearest-neighbor queries in static 2D points

chapters.name: Contest setup
chapters.intro: Start with a compilable single-file submission and fast input.

entries.title: Standalone Main template
entries.when: Start a Java judge submission.
entries.caution: Use the exporter to include required helper classes.

study.idea: Start from a working input/output skeleton so effort stays on the algorithm.
study.example: Read two integers, add them, and print one line.
study.practice: Compile the template before inserting helper classes.

entries.title: Reusable fast input
entries.when: Read large ASCII-token input.
entries.caution: Not a Unicode decoder.

study.idea: Buffered token input reduces per-character overhead on large files.
study.example: Read n, then process exactly n integers with nextInt().
study.practice: Test EOF, negative values, and the final token without a newline.

chapters.name: Fundamentals
chapters.intro: Arrays, windows, sorting, and binary search come first.

entries.title: Loops, arrays, prefix sums, and brute force
entries.when: Process a sequence or test all small pairs.
entries.caution: A prefix array has length n+1 and answers half-open ranges.

study.idea: A direct scan is often the clearest baseline. Prefix sums store the total before each index so one subtraction answers a range.
study.practice: Compare every range sum against a loop on small random arrays.

entries.title: Maps, sets, and stacks
entries.when: Count frequencies, remove duplicates, or check nested delimiters.
entries.complexity: Expected O(n) time for hash collections; O(n) stack space.
entries.caution: HashMap and HashSet have no guaranteed iteration order.

study.idea: A map stores a value for each key, a set stores membership, and a stack reverses the order in which items are processed.
study.example: For [4,2,4], the frequency map stores 4 to 2 and 2 to 1. The string ([{}]) is balanced.
study.practice: Solve a frequency-count problem with both a map and a sorted array, then compare the tradeoffs.

entries.title: Recursion and exhaustive subsets
entries.when: Enumerate all choices when n is small.
entries.caution: Exponential search is only practical for small n; recursion uses stack space.

study.idea: A recursive function solves a smaller instance, reaches a base case, then combines answers. For each subset element, branch into skip and take.
study.example: For [1,2,3] and target 3, subsets [3] and [1,2] both match.
study.practice: Draw the recursion tree for three values and mark its base cases.

entries.title: Arrays and two pointers
entries.when: Use prefix sums, differences, compression, windows, inversions, or permutations.
entries.caution: Sliding-window sums require nonnegative values.

study.idea: Prefix, window, permutation, and inversion patterns replace repeated work with maintained state.
study.example: A nonnegative window can grow right and shrink left while its sum is too large.
study.practice: State the invariant before moving either pointer.

entries.title: Binary search and bounds
entries.when: Search sorted data or a monotone answer predicate.
entries.caution: Sorted input and monotonicity are preconditions.

study.idea: Binary search keeps an interval that is guaranteed to contain the answer.
study.example: For sorted [1, 2, 2, 5], lowerBound(2) is 1 and upperBound(2) is 3.
study.practice: Test an empty array and targets below and above every element.

entries.title: Interval scheduling and covering
entries.when: Select compatible intervals or cover intervals with few points.
entries.caution: Scheduling uses half-open intervals; point covering uses closed intervals.

study.idea: Sort by earliest finishing time. Choosing an early finish leaves as much room as possible for later intervals.
study.example: Among [0,3), [1,2), [2,4), choose the last two.
study.practice: Try to prove the choice by exchanging an optimal first interval with the greedy one.

chapters.name: Range queries and data structures
chapters.intro: Choose by update type, query type, and whether the data changes.

entries.title: DSU, Fenwick, and segment tree
entries.when: Track connectivity, point updates, or range sums.
entries.complexity: Almost O(1) DSU; O(log n) range operations.
entries.caution: Sums use long.

study.idea: Use DSU for merging groups, Fenwick for prefix sums with updates, and segment trees for general ranges.
study.example: After union(0,1), find(0) and find(1) represent the same component.
study.practice: Compare random updates and queries against a plain array.

entries.title: 2D prefix sums, sparse table, lazy tree
entries.when: Answer rectangle sums, immutable minima, or range additions.
entries.complexity: O(1) immutable queries; O(log n) lazy operations.
entries.caution: The sparse table supports idempotent minimum.

study.idea: Preprocessing trades build time and memory for faster repeated queries.
study.example: A rectangle sum uses four 2D prefix values by inclusion-exclusion.
study.practice: Check one-cell, whole-grid, and boundary rectangles.

entries.title: Rollback disjoint set union
entries.when: Undo connectivity merges during offline processing.
entries.caution: No path compression.

study.idea: Record each successful union so it can be reversed.
study.example: Merge 0-1, snapshot, merge 1-2, then roll back to separate 2.
study.practice: Compare snapshots against rebuilt components.

entries.title: Two-dimensional Fenwick tree
entries.when: Update cells and query rectangle sums.
entries.caution: Zero-based half-open rectangles.

study.idea: Nested Fenwick loops aggregate a rectangle through four prefixes.
study.example: Update (1,2), then query a rectangle containing that cell.
study.practice: Compare random rectangles against a matrix.

entries.title: Mo offline distinct queries
entries.when: Answer many static range distinct queries.
entries.caution: All queries must be known in advance.

study.idea: Order queries by left block to limit pointer movement.
study.example: For [1,2,1], distinct [0,3) is 2.
study.practice: Compare with a HashSet on small arrays.

entries.title: Li Chao line container
entries.when: Query the minimum of lines at known coordinates.
entries.caution: Register every x and avoid long overflow.

study.idea: Keep the better line at the midpoint and send the other toward the side where it may win.
study.example: For y=x and y=-x, the minimum at x=3 is -3.
study.practice: Compare against direct line evaluation.

chapters.name: Dynamic programming
chapters.intro: State, transition, base case, and iteration order should be explicit.

entries.title: First dynamic programs
entries.when: Reuse answers to smaller states for sequences, coin change, or grids.
entries.complexity: O(n), O(amount * coin types), or O(rows * columns).
entries.caution: Path counts can overflow long; coin denominations must be positive.

study.idea: Define the state, base case, transition, and answer before writing loops. An iterative table avoids repeated recursion.
study.example: For coins 1, 3, 4, amount 6 needs two coins: 3 + 3.
study.practice: Write a table by hand for a small input and compare it with the program.

entries.title: Classic DP patterns
entries.when: Solve knapsack, subsequence, edit, partition, and counting problems.
entries.caution: Counts can exceed long.

study.idea: Many contest DPs differ only in the state and transition; order must respect dependencies.
study.example: In 0/1 knapsack, iterate capacity downward so an item is used at most once.
study.practice: Write a brute-force subset oracle for small n.

entries.title: Subset, interval, scheduling, digit DP
entries.when: Use richer states than one-dimensional DP.
entries.complexity: O(n^2 2^n), O(n^3), or O(n log n).
entries.caution: Traveling salesperson limits n to 20.

study.idea: Bitmasks, intervals, and digits provide compact state descriptions for harder counting and optimization.
study.example: A TSP mask records visited vertices, while last records the final vertex.
study.practice: Estimate states and memory before allocating a table.

entries.title: Knuth optimized adjacent merging
entries.when: Minimize adjacent merge cost for nonnegative weights.
entries.caution: Split monotonicity depends on this recurrence.

study.idea: Optimal split positions lie between those of neighboring intervals.
study.example: Weights [1,2,3] have optimal cost 9.
study.practice: Compare against cubic interval DP.

chapters.name: Graphs
chapters.intro: Distinguish directed and undirected edges before choosing an algorithm.

entries.title: Adjacency lists, BFS, and grid flood fill
entries.when: Explore an unweighted graph or count regions in a grid.
entries.complexity: O(V+E) for graphs; O(rows * columns) for grids.
entries.caution: For undirected graphs, insert both directions; BFS distance counts edges.

study.idea: An adjacency list stores each vertex's neighbors. BFS visits vertices in layers, so its first visit gives the shortest unweighted distance.
study.example: For edges 0-1 and 1-2, BFS from 0 returns distances 0, 1, 2.
study.practice: Draw a graph with an unreachable vertex and check the returned -1 distance.

entries.title: Traversal, shortest paths, MST
entries.when: Use BFS, DFS, topological order, Dijkstra, or Kruskal.
entries.caution: Dijkstra requires nonnegative weights.

study.idea: Represent edges explicitly, then select traversal or optimization from the weight rules.
study.example: BFS finds unweighted distances; Dijkstra extends this to nonnegative weights.
study.practice: Test disconnected vertices and parallel edges.

entries.title: Components, bipartite, 0-1 BFS, Floyd, Euler
entries.when: Handle graph properties and special shortest paths.
entries.caution: Undirected edges require both directions.

study.idea: Special graph structure can make a hard general problem simpler.
study.example: A deque handles 0-weight edges at the front and 1-weight edges at the back.
study.practice: Compare 0-1 BFS against Dijkstra on small graphs.

entries.title: SCC, Bellman-Ford, LCA, max flow
entries.when: Analyze directed components, negative edges, ancestors, or flow.
entries.complexity: O(V+E) to O(VE), depending on method.
entries.caution: Bellman-Ford rejects reachable negative cycles.

study.idea: SCCs compress directed cycles; flow and ancestor structures answer different global questions.
study.example: Condensing each SCC produces a directed acyclic graph.
study.practice: Draw a graph with two SCCs and one edge between them.

entries.title: Bridges and articulation points
entries.when: Find critical edges or vertices in undirected graphs.
entries.caution: Recursive DFS may exhaust the Java stack.

study.idea: DFS discovery and low-link times reveal edges and vertices whose removal disconnects a graph.
study.example: A tree edge is a bridge when the child cannot reach an ancestor of its parent.
study.practice: Remove each edge in a tiny graph and compare component counts.

entries.title: 2-SAT
entries.when: Solve Boolean formulas with two-literal clauses.
entries.caution: The API uses variable indices and Boolean values.

study.idea: Translate each clause into implications, then test whether a variable and its negation share an SCC.
study.example: The clause a OR b gives implications not-a to b and not-b to a.
study.practice: Enumerate all assignments for formulas with at most ten variables.

entries.title: Minimum-cost flow
entries.when: Optimize flow cost under capacity limits.
entries.complexity: Depends on the number of augmentations.
entries.caution: Initial edge costs must be nonnegative.

study.idea: Residual reverse edges allow a later path to undo an earlier choice.
study.example: After augmenting, add reverse capacity with the negated edge cost.
study.practice: Check a case where rerouting improves the total cost.

entries.title: Bipartite matching and vertex cover
entries.when: Assign left vertices to right vertices.
entries.caution: The DFS phase is recursive.

study.idea: Layered augmenting paths build a maximum matching; alternating reachability gives a minimum cover.
study.example: Edges 0-a, 1-a, 1-b allow a matching of size two.
study.practice: Brute-force tiny matchings and validate the cover.

entries.title: Global minimum cut
entries.when: Find the lightest undirected weighted cut.
entries.caution: Symmetric nonnegative matrix; sums fit long.

study.idea: Stoer-Wagner grows a tight set and contracts its last two vertices.
study.example: Two vertices joined by weight 7 have cut weight 7.
study.practice: Enumerate all vertex subsets on tiny graphs.

entries.title: Exact spanning-tree count
entries.when: Count spanning trees of an undirected multigraph.
entries.caution: Dense exact arithmetic grows quickly; self-loops do not contribute.

study.idea: Kirchhoff removes one row and column of the graph Laplacian and takes the determinant.
study.example: A triangle has three spanning trees.
study.practice: Enumerate edge subsets for small multigraphs.

entries.title: Minimum-cost assignment
entries.when: Assign every worker to a distinct task at minimum total cost.
entries.caution: Dense matrix model; arithmetic overflow is reported.

study.idea: Dual potentials maintain nonnegative reduced costs while augmenting the assignment.
study.example: For [[4,1,3],[2,0,5]], the minimum assignment cost is 3.
study.practice: Compare all column permutations for matrices with at most seven rows.

entries.title: Binary submodular energy minimization
entries.when: Minimize unary label costs plus pairwise submodular penalties.
entries.complexity: Dinic max-flow; runtime depends on graph shape.
entries.caution: Every pair must satisfy E00+E11 <= E01+E10; long arithmetic must fit.

study.idea: Rewrite each pair table as unary terms and a nonnegative directed cut edge.
study.example: A pairwise disagreement penalty encourages adjacent labels to agree.
study.practice: Enumerate all 2^n labelings on small instances and compare energy.

chapters.name: Trees
chapters.intro: Euler order, ancestors, and path decomposition exploit the absence of cycles.

entries.title: Diameter, Euler tour, heavy-light
entries.when: Work with subtree intervals or changing path sums.
entries.complexity: O(n) setup; O(log^2 n) path queries.
entries.caution: Heavy-light setup is recursive and expects a tree.

study.idea: A tree path has unique structure; Euler order turns subtrees into intervals.
study.example: Heavy-light decomposition breaks a path into a logarithmic number of chains.
study.practice: Compare path sums against a simple parent walk on small random trees.

chapters.name: Strings
chapters.intro: Choose a one-pattern, many-pattern, palindrome, or suffix method.

entries.title: Characters, frequencies, and direct matching
entries.when: Count letters, test palindromes, or match a short pattern.
entries.caution: Java char values are UTF-16 code units; the frequency helper accepts a-z only.

study.idea: A string is an indexed sequence. Start with direct comparisons before choosing a faster string algorithm.
study.example: The pattern aa occurs three times in aaaa because matches can overlap.
study.practice: Test an empty text, one character, and overlapping matches.

entries.title: KMP, Manacher, Boyer-Moore, Z
entries.when: Search one pattern or find the longest palindrome.
entries.complexity: Linear for KMP, Manacher, and Z.
entries.caution: Uses Java UTF-16 code units.

study.idea: Prefix, Z, and palindrome arrays summarize repeated character comparisons.
study.example: The prefix function at i gives the longest proper border of the prefix ending at i.
study.practice: Compare matches with direct substring search on random short strings.

entries.title: Trie and rolling hash
entries.when: Store prefixes or compare substrings quickly.
entries.complexity: O(total characters) build; O(1) hash query.
entries.caution: Hash equality is probabilistic.

study.idea: A trie shares common prefixes; rolling hash compresses a substring into modular values.
study.example: Words car and cat share the c-a prefix nodes in a trie.
study.practice: Use direct string comparison when a hash collision would be unacceptable.

entries.title: Suffix array and LCP
entries.when: Order suffixes or count distinct substrings.
entries.complexity: O(n log^2 n) array; O(n) LCP.
entries.caution: Comparison sorting is simple but slower.

study.idea: Sorting suffixes turns substring questions into adjacent comparisons.
study.example: Every repeated substring appears as a prefix of at least two neighboring suffixes.
study.practice: Compare distinct-substring counts against a set of all substrings for short text.

entries.title: Aho-Corasick
entries.when: Match many patterns against text.
entries.complexity: Linear in text and automaton size.
entries.caution: Lowercase a-z only.

study.idea: Failure links let multiple pattern searches share work while scanning text once.
study.example: Patterns he and she can both finish during a scan of she.
study.practice: Test duplicate patterns and patterns that are suffixes of other patterns.

entries.title: Minimum cyclic rotation
entries.when: Find a lexicographically smallest rotation.
entries.caution: Uses Java UTF-16 code units.

study.idea: Booth discards candidate starts after each mismatch.
study.example: The minimum rotation of bba is abb.
study.practice: Compare all rotations on short strings.

entries.title: Suffix automaton
entries.when: Count distinct substrings or find a longest common substring.
entries.caution: HashMap transitions use UTF-16 code units.

study.idea: Clone states preserve suffix links when an equivalence class splits.
study.example: The string aba has five distinct nonempty substrings.
study.practice: Compare against a set of all short substrings.

chapters.name: Number theory and combinatorics
chapters.intro: Use exact or modular arithmetic according to the requested result.

entries.title: GCD, trial division, divisors, and powers
entries.when: Solve small divisibility and integer arithmetic tasks.
entries.complexity: GCD O(log n); trial division O(sqrt n); power O(log exponent).
entries.caution: Exact power reports long overflow; inputs to gcd must be nonnegative.

study.idea: A divisor larger than the square root has a matching smaller divisor. Euclid repeatedly replaces (a,b) by (b,a mod b).
study.example: The divisors of 36 come in pairs around 6, giving nine positive divisors.
study.practice: Compare trial-division results with direct enumeration for small values.

entries.title: GCD, modular arithmetic, primality, CRT
entries.when: Work with divisibility, primes, congruences, or roots.
entries.complexity: Euclid O(log n); sieve O(n log log n).
entries.caution: Overflow-safe modular multiplication trades speed for range.

study.idea: Choose the correct number representation and modulus before applying arithmetic routines.
study.example: Euclid finds gcd; the extended form also gives coefficients for modular inverses.
study.practice: Compare modular operations against BigInteger on boundary inputs.

entries.title: Factors, phi, inverse, modular nCr, matrices
entries.when: Factor integers or exponentiate recurrences.
entries.complexity: O(sqrt n) factorization; O(k^3 log exponent) matrices.
entries.caution: PrimeCombinations needs a prime modulus greater than its limit.

study.idea: Precomputation pays off when many factor or binomial queries share the same limits.
study.example: A smallest-prime-factor table decomposes 84 as 2 squared times 3 times 7.
study.practice: Compare factorization and totient against direct small-number implementations.

entries.title: Exact binomial and Catalan numbers
entries.when: Compute counts beyond long range.
entries.caution: BigInteger is exact but allocates memory.

study.idea: BigInteger keeps exact counts when the answer does not fit a primitive type.
study.example: The number of ways to choose 2 from 5 is 10.
study.practice: Check symmetry C(n,k) = C(n,n-k).

entries.title: Discrete log, modular root, Mobius
entries.when: Solve multiplicative congruences and inversion problems.
entries.complexity: O(sqrt modulus) discrete log; O(n) Mobius sieve.
entries.caution: Discrete log needs a coprime base; roots need a prime modulus.

study.idea: Baby-step giant-step trades memory for speed; Tonelli-Shanks extracts roots.
study.example: Modulo 7, 3 squared equals 2.
study.practice: Compare against exhaustive small powers and squares.

entries.title: Derangements, Stirling, partitions, Burnside
entries.when: Count permutations, set partitions, and necklaces.
entries.complexity: O(n) to O(n sqrt n) BigInteger work.
entries.caution: Exact answers can become very large.

study.idea: Recurrences and Burnside count objects without enumerating them.
study.example: There are 44 derangements of five items.
study.practice: Enumerate tiny objects and compare counts.

chapters.name: Polynomial methods
chapters.intro: Convolution accelerates counting and polynomial tasks.

entries.title: Number-theoretic transform
entries.when: Multiply large polynomials modulo 998244353.
entries.caution: Transform length must not exceed 2^23.

study.idea: A transform changes polynomial multiplication into pointwise multiplication under a suitable prime.
study.example: Coefficients [1,2] times [3,4] become [3,10,8].
study.practice: Compare small random convolutions against the quadratic method.

chapters.name: Numerical methods
chapters.intro: Solve dense systems, multiply polynomials, and use transforms when their assumptions fit.

entries.title: Gaussian elimination and determinant
entries.when: Solve dense real systems or compute determinants.
entries.caution: Absolute epsilon can misclassify near-singular systems.

study.idea: Pivot on the largest coefficient and eliminate the column.
study.example: Equations 2x+y=5 and x-y=1 give x=2, y=1.
study.practice: Multiply the solution back and check residuals.

entries.title: Subset zeta, Mobius, and XOR transforms
entries.when: Aggregate values over all submasks or XOR combinations.
entries.caution: Array length must be a power of two; long sums may overflow.

study.idea: Each bit doubles the group of masks that contributes to an aggregate.
study.example: For f[0]=1 and f[1]=2, zeta gives [1,3].
study.practice: Compare every transformed mask with direct submask enumeration.

entries.title: Fast Fourier transform convolution
entries.when: Multiply long coefficient arrays when floating-point rounding is safe.
entries.complexity: O(n log n) for a power-of-two padded length.
entries.caution: Floating-point rounding is approximate; use NTT for exact modular answers.

study.idea: The FFT turns polynomial multiplication into pointwise multiplication in frequency space.
study.example: The convolution of [1,2] and [3,4] is [3,10,8].
study.practice: Compare with quadratic multiplication using small coefficients.

chapters.name: Geometry
chapters.intro: Use floating-point distances and exact integer predicates as appropriate.

entries.title: Distance, polygons, hull, closest pair
entries.when: Measure and optimize among planar points.
entries.caution: Floating-point orientation is unstable near collinearity.

study.idea: Sort and orient points carefully; choose exact predicates when coordinates are integral.
study.example: A convex hull removes interior points before farthest-pair search.
study.practice: Test duplicate and collinear points.

entries.title: Exact orientation and intersection
entries.when: Need robust integer geometry predicates.
entries.caution: BigInteger avoids overflow but allocates.

study.idea: Compute cross products with BigInteger so integer orientation never silently overflows.
study.example: The sign of the cross product distinguishes left turn, right turn, and collinearity.
study.practice: Test segments sharing an endpoint and nearly collinear large coordinates.

entries.title: Lines, segments, and circle intersections
entries.when: Measure distances or intersect lines and circles.
entries.caution: Coincident circles have infinitely many intersections.

study.idea: Projection and the common chord solve these primitives.
study.example: Unit circles centered at (0,0) and (2,0) touch at (1,0).
study.practice: Test tangent, disjoint, and degenerate cases.

entries.title: Two-dimensional KD-tree nearest neighbor
entries.when: Find the nearest point repeatedly in a static 2D point set.
entries.complexity: O(n log^2 n) build; average O(log n), worst O(n) per query.
entries.caution: Worst-case query is linear and squared distances can overflow double.

study.idea: Alternating coordinate partitions create boxes that can be pruned by distance lower bounds.
study.example: For points (0,0) and (4,0), query (3,0) returns the second point.
study.practice: Compare random queries with a full scan and include duplicate points.

entries.title: 3D vectors and spherical distance
entries.when: Compute vector products, tetrahedron volume, or distance on a sphere.
entries.caution: Latitude uses degrees; spherical distance assumes a mean Earth radius.

study.idea: Dot and cross products extend orientation and area calculations to three dimensions.
study.example: The cross product of (1,0,0) and (0,1,0) is (0,0,1).
study.practice: Check orthogonality with dot products and compare great-circle distances with known locations.

chapters.name: Game theory
chapters.intro: Model legal moves and terminal states before applying xor or mex.

entries.title: Nim, mex, Grundy, minimax
entries.when: Analyze impartial games or complete binary game trees.
entries.caution: Nim assumes normal play.

study.idea: For impartial normal-play games, a zero xor of Grundy values is losing.
study.example: Nim heaps of sizes 1, 2, and 3 have xor zero.
study.practice: Enumerate all moves in a tiny game to verify Grundy labels.

beginner.audience: Teams learning to turn a problem statement into loops, data structures, and a correct first solution.
beginner.prerequisites: Java variables, methods, arrays, loops, conditionals, and basic input/output.
goals: Read constraints and estimate whether O(n), O(n log n), or O(n^2) fits.
Implement and test simple loops, prefix sums, sorting, and direct search.
Recognize a correct greedy choice and the four parts of a dynamic program.
Represent a graph and use BFS for unweighted distances.
beginner.practice: For each pattern, solve one small problem directly, test empty and boundary inputs, then explain the invariant in one sentence.

intermediate.audience: Teams comfortable with basics and ready to select standard algorithms under contest constraints.
intermediate.prerequisites: The beginner reference, asymptotic notation, sorting, BFS, and simple dynamic programming.
goals: Choose between static prefix queries and update-capable trees.
State graph direction and weight assumptions before selecting a path algorithm.
Design DP states, transitions, and iteration order.
Use string matching and number theory with explicit numeric bounds.
Use offline queries, bipartite matching, and circle primitives.
Solve dense assignment problems and use three-dimensional vector operations.
intermediate.practice: Compare a fast method against a brute-force oracle on random small cases; record the first failing seed.

advanced.audience: Teams preparing for problems that combine several techniques or require specialized algorithms.
advanced.prerequisites: The intermediate reference, graph traversal, DP, modular arithmetic, and proof by invariant.
goals: Recognize reductions to flows, satisfiability, tree paths, and convolution.
Check hidden assumptions such as negative costs and recursion depth.
Estimate both asymptotic cost and Java memory overhead.
Validate complex algorithms with adversarial and differential tests.
Check specialized data structures and numerical preconditions before use.
Model submodular binary energies as graph cuts and select FFT or NTT by precision needs.
advanced.practice: For each advanced method, write the invariant and construct a small case that breaks an incorrect implementation.

beginner.title: Read constraints before coding
beginner.idea: A solution is useful only when it fits the input size. One loop over n items is O(n); nested loops over every pair are O(n^2). Sorting is usually O(n log n). Exponential subset enumeration becomes expensive quickly.
beginner.example: At n = 2,000, trying roughly four million pairs may be reasonable; at n = 200,000, forty billion pairs are not. Check the actual time limit and Java overhead.
beginner.exercise: For each problem, write n and a rough operation count next to the proposed approach.

beginner.title: Move from a baseline to a faster method
beginner.idea: First state a simple correct method. Identify repeated work, then reuse it with a prefix array, sorted order, a map, or a maintained state. Keep the baseline as a test oracle for tiny cases.
beginner.example: Summing each query interval with a loop costs O(length). Building prefix sums once costs O(n), then each interval needs one subtraction.
beginner.exercise: Implement both methods and compare every interval on a short random array.

beginner.title: State the invariant
beginner.idea: An invariant describes what remains true after each loop step. It helps prove that a scan, binary search, queue, or greedy choice is correct.
beginner.example: During BFS, every queued vertex has a known shortest distance, and vertices leave the queue in nondecreasing distance.
beginner.exercise: Explain why the first discovered path to a vertex has the fewest edges.

beginner.title: Check boundaries systematically
beginner.idea: Test the smallest legal size, empty containers when permitted, duplicate values, negative values, and the largest numeric result. Keep zero-based indices and half-open ranges explicit.
beginner.example: For prefix sums of three values, prefix has four entries; the whole array is [0,3), and an empty range is [2,2).
beginner.exercise: Write tests for an empty array, one value, and a range ending at n.

intermediate.title: Select by operations, not by name
intermediate.idea: A data structure is defined by the updates and queries it supports. Prefix sums answer static sums. Fenwick trees handle point updates and prefix sums. Lazy trees handle range updates.
intermediate.example: If queries ask for sums after changing one index, a static prefix array requires rebuilding; a Fenwick tree changes O(log n) cells.
intermediate.exercise: List the update and query type before choosing a data structure.

intermediate.title: Design a dynamic program
intermediate.idea: Write the state meaning, base cases, transition, iteration order, and output location. Check whether the transition reuses a state from the current iteration.
intermediate.example: In 0/1 knapsack, descending capacity prevents using one item twice; ascending capacity instead models unbounded use.
intermediate.exercise: Derive a small table by hand and compare with the implementation.

intermediate.title: Match graph assumptions to algorithms
intermediate.idea: Unweighted edges favor BFS, 0/1 weights favor deque-based BFS, nonnegative weights permit Dijkstra, and negative weights require a different method. Directedness and disconnected vertices also matter.
intermediate.example: A weight of -1 invalidates Dijkstra even if most edges are positive.
intermediate.exercise: For each graph problem, write direction, weight range, number of vertices, and number of edges.

advanced.title: Recognize the reduction
advanced.idea: Advanced problems often hide a standard model. Decide whether the objects are vertices, intervals, states, Boolean literals, flow units, or polynomial coefficients.
advanced.example: Choosing compatible assignments with pairwise either-or constraints may become 2-SAT; routing units at minimum total cost may become min-cost flow.
advanced.exercise: Describe the model and prove each problem constraint is represented exactly once.

advanced.title: Budget both asymptotics and memory
advanced.idea: In Java, an O(n^2) table may be limited by object headers and array references as well as cell count. Recursive graph traversals may hit the call stack before time becomes a problem.
advanced.example: A 2^20 by 20 long table contains about 160 MiB of values before array overhead.
advanced.exercise: Estimate bytes and calls for the largest case before selecting an implementation.

advanced.title: Validate the difficult invariant
advanced.idea: Use a slower oracle on small inputs, preserve failing seeds, and include adversarial cases. State preconditions such as nonnegative initial costs, prime modulus, and coordinate range.
advanced.example: Compare an NTT product with O(nm) multiplication for random short polynomials.
advanced.exercise: Construct a case with duplicates, disconnected components, or a later residual reroute.

beginner.title: Answer many range sums
beginner.task: Given values [3, -2, 5, 4], answer sums for half-open ranges [1,3) and [0,4).
beginner.reason: Build prefix [0,3,1,6,10]. A range [l,r) is prefix[r] - prefix[l], so the answers are 6 - 3 and 10 - 0.
beginner.cost: O(n) build and O(1) per query.
beginner.check: Compare against a loop for all ranges, including [2,2) and [0,4).

beginner.title: Choose compatible activities
beginner.task: Given [0,3), [1,2), [2,4), and [4,5), choose the maximum number of non-overlapping intervals.
beginner.reason: Sort by ending time. Choose [1,2), then [2,4), then [4,5). Choosing [0,3) first would leave less room.
beginner.check: Enumerate all subsets for four intervals and confirm no larger compatible set exists.

beginner.title: Count rooms in a grid
beginner.task: Treat # as open in the three rows #.#, #.., and .##. Count four-neighbor connected regions.
beginner.reason: Start a BFS at each unseen open cell. The top-left pair is one region, the top-right cell another, and the bottom-right pair a third.
beginner.cost: O(rows * columns), because each cell is visited at most once.
beginner.check: Replace the center wall with an open cell and recount the connected regions.

beginner.title: Find the minimum number of coins
beginner.task: With unlimited coins of values 1, 3, and 4, form amount 6 using as few coins as possible.
beginner.reason: Let dp[x] be the best answer for amount x. For each coin c <= x, try dp[x-c] + 1. The best choice is 3 + 3.
beginner.check: Try amount 0, an unreachable amount without coin 1, and a greedy counterexample such as amount 6.

intermediate.title: Maintain merging teams
intermediate.task: Start with vertices 0 through 3. Merge (0,1), (2,3), then (1,2). Ask whether 0 and 3 are connected.
intermediate.reason: Each union joins two representative components. After the third union, all four vertices share one representative.
intermediate.cost: Almost constant amortized time per operation.
intermediate.check: Compare every connectivity query with BFS on the edges inserted so far.

intermediate.title: Use weighted shortest paths
intermediate.task: Directed edges are 0 to 1 with weight 4, 0 to 2 with weight 1, and 2 to 1 with weight 1. Find the distance from 0 to 1.
intermediate.reason: The direct path costs 4. The route through vertex 2 costs 1 + 1. All weights are nonnegative, so Dijkstra applies.
intermediate.cost: O((V+E) log V) with a priority queue.
intermediate.check: Add a disconnected vertex and confirm it retains the unreachable sentinel.

intermediate.title: Choose items once
intermediate.task: Weights are [2,3,4], values are [4,5,6], and capacity is 5. Maximize total value with each item used at most once.
intermediate.reason: Choose the first two items for weight 5 and value 9. Update capacity downward so the current item cannot be reused.
intermediate.check: Enumerate all eight subsets and compare their feasible values.

advanced.title: Translate clauses into implications
advanced.task: Find values of a and b satisfying (a or b), (not a or b), and (not b or a).
advanced.result: a = true and b = true is a solution
advanced.reason: For each clause x or y, add not x to y and not y to x. Solve the implication graph by SCC and reject if a variable meets its negation.
advanced.check: Enumerate all four assignments to confirm the returned solution satisfies every clause.

advanced.title: Multiply two polynomials
advanced.reason: The coefficients come from convolution: 1*3, then 1*4 + 2*3, then 2*4. NTT makes the same operation efficient for long arrays.
advanced.cost: O(n log n) for a padded transform of length n.
advanced.check: Compare random short arrays against nested-loop multiplication.

advanced.title: Route flow at minimum cost
advanced.task: Send two units from 0 to 3. Edges 0-1 and 1-3 have cost 1 and capacity 1; edges 0-2 and 2-3 have costs 2 and 1 with capacity 1.
advanced.reason: One unit takes 0-1-3 at cost 2. The other takes 0-2-3 at cost 3. Residual reverse edges allow later augmentations to revise a choice.
advanced.cost: Depends on the number of augmenting paths and shortest-path work.
advanced.check: Verify delivered flow, capacity limits, and the sum of used edge costs.
